concept.name: Consumer price index
concept.definition: A measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services, published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The headline series is the CPI for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).
concept.intuition: The CPI is a giant shopping basket whose total cost is tracked every month; how fast that basket's cost rises is the most-watched U.S. inflation reading.
concept.mechanics: BLS collects prices for thousands of items across urban areas, weights them by consumer spending patterns from the Consumer Expenditure Surveys, and aggregates them into an index (reference base 1982-84=100). Monthly releases report seasonally adjusted month-over-month and unadjusted 12-month changes, including the 'all items less food and energy' core series.
concept.formula: Percent change = (Index_t / Index_{t-1} - 1) x 100; the index itself is a weighted average of item-level price relatives with expenditure weights.
concept.failure_modes: CPI covers only urban consumers' out-of-pocket spending, uses owners' equivalent rent for housing, and embeds substitution and quality-adjustment assumptions, so it can diverge from any household's lived inflation and from the Fed's preferred PCE measure.
concept.misconceptions: The CPI is not a cost-of-living index in the strict sense and does not measure price levels across cities; a higher index in one period means prices rose, not that every item did.
concept.example: In June 2026, BLS reported CPI-U fell 0.4% month over month (seasonally adjusted) while rising 3.5% over 12 months — the 12-month figure is the headline inflation rate.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index (CPI Home)
